The wrong pair is (4) Chess – Outdoor game.

The chapter lists chess among the indoor games. Indoor games are played within a closed environment and a number of them are played sitting at one place; they include chess, card games, games played with gamesmen and dice, and carom.

The other three pairs are correct: mallakhamb is listed among the outdoor sports based on physical skills, water polo among the water sports, and skating among the adventurous sports.

Toys are the means and equipment for the entertainment and education of children, and they can throw light on history and on technological development. We also get a glimpse of religious and cultural traditions through them.

The chapter's example is Diwali in Maharashtra. As a part of the traditional Diwali celebrations model forts are made, and clay images of Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj and his soldiers, and of people and animals, are placed on these model forts. This tradition keeps alive the memory of the important role of forts in the history of Maharashtra.

In this way a toy made for a festival carries a piece of history forward from one generation to the next.

Recently some movies on sports and on the biographies of players have been released in various languages.

The chapter gives two examples. Mary Kom is about the first Indian female boxer to participate in the Olympics and win a bronze medal. Dangal is based on the life story of the Foghat sisters, who were the first Indian female wrestlers to win gold medals at various international competitions.

Movies of this kind belong with the other sports literature the chapter describes — the recently published history of Mallakhamb, an encyclopaedia on the subject of exercise, the sports magazine 'Shatkar' and the television channels devoted exclusively to sports.

The field of sports in the 20th-21st century was influenced by the process of globalisation. International matches of cricket, football and lawn tennis can now be watched on television in any corner of the world, so that citizens of non-participant countries can also enjoy them — the chapter's example is the world cup winning match played by Indian cricketers, watched by cricket fans all over the world.

Because sports fans are now scattered all over the world, the entire structure of the sports economy has been significantly affected. Fans watch the matches for entertainment; industrial and commercial companies look at them as a good opportunity to advertise their wares; and retired sportsmen get an opportunity to participate as commentators.

Toys can throw light on history and technological development, and we can get a glimpse of religious and cultural traditions through them.

Clay toys have been found in archaeological excavations, fashioned either by hand or by using moulds, so they tell us how they were made and with what skill. The model forts made in Maharashtra at Diwali, with clay images of Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj and his soldiers, keep alive the memory of the role of forts in the history of Maharashtra.

Toys can also show contact between cultures. An ivory doll made by Indian craftsmen was found in the excavation of Pompeii in Italy and is dated to the 1st century C.E.; that artefact throws light on Indo-Roman trade relations. Toys found in archaeological excavations can therefore tell us about cultural contacts between nations in ancient times.

The means and equipment for the entertainment and education of children are called toys. Clay toys have been found in archaeological excavations, and they were fashioned either by hand or by using moulds.

Dolls are mentioned in ancient Indian literature: a Sanskrit play by Shudraka is named Mrichchhakatika, which means a clay cart. In India there are regional traditions of making dolls, and the wooden dolls made in Maharashtra were known as Thaki.

Ancient Indian literature and the epics also mention various games such as the game of dice (dyut), wrestling, horse and chariot races and chess, so the equipment for these games is equally old. Kathasaritsagara has very interesting descriptions of games and toys.

Toys of this kind are historical evidence. The ivory doll made by Indian craftsmen found in the excavation of Pompeii in Italy, dated to the 1st century C.E., throws light on Indo-Roman trade relations.

[Note: the chapter describes toys, dolls and the games mentioned in ancient literature, but it does not give a dated sequence of sports equipment in ancient India beyond these examples.]

Although sports and history appear to be distant as subjects, there is a close tie between them.

Students of history can find many opportunities in the field of sports journalism, because one has to resort to history in order to write articles and reviews about sports events such as the Olympics, the Asiad and national and international matches. Expert commentators are in demand during matches, and a commentator needs good knowledge of the history, statistics, previous records, eminent players and historical anecdotes related to the game concerned.

Knowledge of the history of sports is also essential for writing articles in publications such as encyclopaedias, newspapers and sports magazines, and for research of this kind.

Toys and game materials tie the two subjects together from the other side: they throw light on history and technological development, on religious and cultural traditions, and even on contacts between nations, as the ivory doll of Indian make found at Pompeii shows.

The chapter says sports are of two types, Indoor Games and Outdoor Games.

Indoor games are played within a closed environment, and a number of them are played sitting at one place. They include chess, card games, games played with gamesmen and dice, and carom. Kachkavadya or Chaukabara, also known as Indian Ludo, is very popular among Indians; Sagargote, played with a bunch of seeds or stones, and Bhatukali (playing house) are usually played by girls, though in Bhatukali all the members of the family can join in, especially in the mock wedding of a girl doll and a boy doll.

Outdoor games are categorised into two types, Indian sports and International sports. Indian games include Langadi, Kabaddi, Atyapatya and Kho-kho, and popular Indian games also include marbles, Lagori, Vitti-Dandu or Gilli-Danda, Bhingari (whorls), Bhovare (tops), Phugadi and Zimma. The international games include Badminton, Table Tennis, Hockey, Cricket, Football, Golf and Polo. Running races — sprints of 100 and 200 metres, middle and long distance races, the marathon, hurdles and relays — are popular all over the world, and shot put, discus throw, long jump, high jump, water sports such as swimming, water polo and rowing, and sports combining physical exercise with acrobatics such as mallakhamb, rope mallakhamb and gymnastics are all outdoor sports based on physical skills.
